examTitle: Our Common Bond Australian Practice Exam
dossierParchmentText: Whereas the people of New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Queensland, and Tasmania, humbly relying on the blessing of Almighty God, have agreed to unite in one indissoluble Federal Commonwealth under the Crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and under the Constitution hereby established...

questions.category: Australia’s Democratic Beliefs & Rights
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 1
questions.questionText: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the planned federal capital territory established in 1913.

options.text: Sydney
Melbourne
Canberra
Brisbane

statutoryGuidance.clue: Chosen as a compromise between rival cities Sydney and Melbourne.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Seat of Government Act 1908
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Canberra = Capital of Australia (ACT).
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Canberra houses Parliament House, the High Court of Australia, and the National Gallery in the Australian Capital Territory.

questions.category: Australian Values (Mandatory)
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 4 (Mandatory Values)
questions.questionText: In Australia, what does the value of "equality of men and women" mean under the law?
questions.subtext: Select the mandatory Australian value regarding gender equality and legal rights.

options.text: Men and women have identical rights, freedoms, and protections
Men hold primary authority in domestic and family disputes
Women must obtain family permission before seeking employment
Legal protections vary depending on cultural or ethnic background

statutoryGuidance.clue: Australian law guarantees complete equality regardless of gender.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth)
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Equal Rights: Men and women have equal opportunities and dignity.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Australian Values questions are zero-tolerance: applicants must answer all five values questions correctly to pass the DHA examination.

questions.category: Australia and Its People
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: Who are the original Indigenous peoples of Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the two distinct Aboriginal cultures possessing ancient heritage.

options.text: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Maori and Polynesian peoples
Melanesian and Micronesian settlers
Inuit and First Nations peoples

statutoryGuidance.clue: Possessing the oldest continuous living cultures in the world, spanning over 65,000 years.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: National Indigenous Australians Agency Protocols
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: ATSI: Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander peoples.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Aboriginal peoples mainland Australia and Torres Strait Islanders from northern islands possess rich traditions, Dreamtime stories, and connection to land.

questions.category: Australian Values (Mandatory)
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 4 (Mandatory Values)
questions.questionText: Should people in Australia be allowed to express their opinions peacefully without fear?
questions.subtext: Determine the scope of freedom of speech and expression in Australian society.

options.text: Yes, freedom of speech is a fundamental value within the law
No, only opinions endorsed by the government are permitted
Only media journalists have the right to speak publicly
Speech must be approved in advance by local police

statutoryGuidance.clue: Australians value peaceful open debate, free expression, and mutual respect.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Common Law · Implied Freedom of Political Communication
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Freedom of Speech allows peaceful sharing of differing views.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: While expression is free, it must operate within the law—incitement to violence or racial vilification is prohibited.

questions.category: Government and the Law in Australia
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 3
questions.questionText: Who is the King’s representative in Australia at the federal level?
questions.subtext: Identify the viceregal head of state under the Australian Constitution.

options.text: The Governor-General
The Prime Minister
The High Court Chief Justice
The Premier of New South Wales

statutoryGuidance.clue: Appointed by the Sovereign on the recommendation of the Australian Prime Minister.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Constitution, ss. 2 & 61
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Governor-General acts on behalf of the King in Australia.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Under the Australian Constitution, executive power is vested in the King and exercisable by the Governor-General.

questions.category: Australian Values (Mandatory)
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 4 (Mandatory Values)
questions.questionText: What does "a fair go" mean in Australian society?
questions.subtext: Identify the iconic Australian cultural ethos regarding equality and opportunity.

options.text: Everyone deserves equal opportunity and fair treatment
Wealthy individuals receive priority judicial hearings
All citizens must earn the identical annual salary
Only native-born citizens may access public healthcare

statutoryGuidance.clue: A defining national concept: giving everyone a fair chance regardless of background.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Our Common Bond · Core Cultural Value: "A Fair Go"
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: A Fair Go = Equality of opportunity, dignity, and compassion.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The "fair go" reflects Australia’s egalitarian spirit, valuing hard work and mutual respect over inherited class privilege.

questions.category: Australian Values (Mandatory)
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 4 (Mandatory Values)
questions.questionText: In Australia, are people free to follow any religion or no religion at all?
questions.subtext: Select the principle governing freedom of religion in the Commonwealth.

options.text: Yes, freedom of religion is protected and people may choose any or no faith
No, everyone must register with an official church
Only religions established before 1901 are lawful
Religious leaders can overrule civil criminal statutes

statutoryGuidance.clue: Section 116 of the Constitution bars the federal government from establishing any religion.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Constitution, s. 116
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Section 116 = Freedom of religion and secular democracy.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Australians are free to practice any peaceful religion or choose no faith, but religious laws never override Australian law.

questions.category: Australian Values (Mandatory)
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 4 (Mandatory Values)
questions.questionText: Is it acceptable to use violence towards a family member or partner in Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the mandatory zero-tolerance legal standard concerning domestic violence.

options.text: No, domestic and family violence is strictly illegal in Australia
Yes, if permitted by religious or traditional customs
Yes, in private domestic disputes between married spouses
Only minor physical punishment is allowed without police charges

statutoryGuidance.clue: Domestic and family violence is never acceptable and is punishable under criminal law.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Family Law Act 1975 & State Criminal Codes
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Zero tolerance: Violence of any kind is a serious crime.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Australian law strictly forbids all physical, emotional, and financial abuse against any partner or child, with no cultural exemptions.

questions.category: Government and the Law in Australia
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 3
questions.questionText: Voting in federal and state elections in Australia is:
questions.subtext: Determine the statutory legal requirement for Australian citizens aged 18 and over.

options.text: Compulsory for all eligible citizens
Voluntary for everyone
Only compulsory for registered party members
Mandatory only for landowners and businesses

statutoryGuidance.clue: Australia was one of the first democracies to introduce compulsory voting (1924).
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918, s. 245
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Voting is Compulsory: every eligible citizen must cast a ballot.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Compulsory voting ensures that governments are elected by a true majority of all eligible adult citizens.

questions.category: Australian Symbols & National Days
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: On what date is Australia Day celebrated each year?
questions.subtext: Identify the national holiday marking the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788.

options.text: 26 January
25 April
1 January
11 November

statutoryGuidance.clue: Marks the raising of the British flag at Sydney Cove by Captain Arthur Phillip in 1788.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australia Day Public Holiday Acts
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: 26 January = Australia Day; 25 April = Anzac Day.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Australia Day is celebrated with citizenship ceremonies, community awards, and reflection on national history.

questions.category: Australian History • Anzac Tradition
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: What does Anzac Day commemorate on 25 April each year?
questions.subtext: Identify the sacred military remembrance day marking the 1915 landing at Gallipoli.

options.text: The landing of Australian and New Zealand forces at Gallipoli in 1915
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The declaration of Federation in Sydney
The end of the second World War in the Pacific

statutoryGuidance.clue: ANZAC: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Anzac Day Commemoration Acts
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: 25 April: Dawn Services honoring all military personnel who served and died.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The Anzac spirit represents courage, endurance, initiative, and mateship forged on the shores of Turkey in 1915.

questions.category: Government and the Law in Australia
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 3
questions.questionText: What are the two houses of the Federal Parliament of Australia?
questions.subtext: Select the upper and lower federal legislative chambers.

options.text: The Senate and the House of Representatives
The Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly
The Privy Council and High Chamber
The National Assembly and Congress

statutoryGuidance.clue: Green chamber is the House of Representatives; red chamber is the Senate.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Constitution, s. 1
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Federal Parliament = Senate (76 senators) + House of Reps (151 MPs).
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The House of Representatives forms the government; the Senate provides equal representation for the six founding states.

questions.category: Australian Symbols & Heritage
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: What is the national anthem of Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the anthem adopted in 1984.

options.text: Advance Australia Fair
Waltzing Matilda
God Save the King
I Still Call Australia Home

statutoryGuidance.clue: Opening words: "Australians all let us rejoice, for we are one and free".
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Proclamation of National Anthem (1984, amended 2021)
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Advance Australia Fair: "one and free".
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The anthem was amended in 2021 from "for we are young and free" to "for we are one and free" to recognize Indigenous history.

questions.category: Australian History • Federation
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: In what year did the six British colonies unite to form the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the Federation year celebrated on 1 January.

statutoryGuidance.clue: Federation occurred on January 1, 1901, with Edmund Barton as the first Prime Minister.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: 1901: Federation united the 6 colonies into one nation.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Federation established a national federal government while retaining state parliaments for local matters.

questions.category: Government and the Law in Australia
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 3
questions.questionText: What is the highest court in the Australian judicial system?
questions.subtext: Select the constitutional court located in Canberra.

options.text: The High Court of Australia
The Federal Court of Australia
The Supreme Court of New South Wales
The Privy Council

statutoryGuidance.clue: Consists of the Chief Justice and six other Justices interpreting the Constitution.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Constitution, s. 71 & Judiciary Act 1903
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: High Court of Australia = Final court of appeal.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The High Court decides constitutional challenges and hears appeals from federal and state appellate courts.

questions.category: Australian Geography & States
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: How many states and major mainland territories are there in Australia?
questions.subtext: Determine the count of federated states and mainland territories.

options.text: 6 States and 2 Mainland Territories
7 States and 3 Territories
5 States and 1 Territory
8 States and 2 Territories

statutoryGuidance.clue: States: NSW, VIC, QLD, WA, SA, TAS. Mainland Territories: ACT and NT.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Constitution & Territory Self-Government Acts
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: 6 States + 2 Mainland Territories (ACT & NT).
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The six founding states have individual state constitutions and parliaments.

questions.category: Australian Symbols • National Colours
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: What are the official national colours of Australia?
questions.subtext: Identify the iconic sports and ceremonial colours.

options.text: Green and Gold
Red and White
Blue and Silver
Black and Ochre

statutoryGuidance.clue: Inspired by the golden wattle flower against green foliage, proclaimed in 1984.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Governor-General Proclamation of National Colours (1984)
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Green & Gold = Australia’s official national colours.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Green and gold represent the golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha), Australia’s national floral emblem.

questions.category: Government and the Law in Australia
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 3
questions.questionText: Who forms the Government in the Australian federal parliament?
questions.subtext: Identify how the executive government is determined following a general election.

options.text: The party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives
The party that wins the highest number of Senate seats
Appointed directly by the Governor-General without party affiliation
Chosen by a nationwide vote of all municipal city mayors

statutoryGuidance.clue: 76 of the 151 House of Representatives seats are needed to form majority government.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Westminster System Conventions & Australian Constitution
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Majority in the House of Representatives = Forms Government.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The leader of the majority party becomes Prime Minister, and ministers are chosen from members of Parliament.

questions.category: Australian Symbols • Coat of Arms
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 2
questions.questionText: Which two native Australian animals support the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.subtext: Identify the kangaroo and flightless bird chosen because they rarely move backwards.

options.text: The Kangaroo and the Emu
The Koala and the Platypus
The Dingo and the Wombat
The Kookaburra and the Tasmanian Devil

statutoryGuidance.clue: Both animals symbolize a nation moving forward, incapable of walking backwards easily.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Royal Warrant granting Commonwealth Arms (1912)
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Kangaroo + Emu: Looking forward.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The Australian Coat of Arms shows a shield with the badges of the six states supported by a red kangaroo and an emu.

questions.category: Australia’s Democratic Beliefs & Rights
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · Section 1
questions.questionText: What is a key privilege and responsibility granted to new Australian citizens?
questions.subtext: Identify the democratic and civic right acquired upon taking the pledge.

options.text: The right to vote and hold an Australian passport
Exemption from municipal council taxes
Automatic free travel on commercial international airlines
Immunity from civil contract litigation

statutoryGuidance.clue: New citizens gain voting rights, an Australian passport, and the right to stand for public office.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth)
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: Citizenship = Voting + Passport + Civic Participation.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: By making the Australian Citizenship Pledge, citizens affirm loyalty to Australia, its democratic beliefs, and laws.

questions.subtext: Identify the official capital city of New South Wales.

Darwin
Sydney
Perth

statutoryGuidance.clue: The capital city of New South Wales is Sydney.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond (DHA), Part 1: Australia and Its People
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: New South Wales capital: Sydney.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Sydney is the administrative capital and seat of government for New South Wales.

Separated from NSW in 1859

statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: Historical establishment of New South Wales contributed to the federation of Australian colonies in 1901.

questions.category: Australian Government • Constitutional Status
questions.statutoryStandard: Our Common Bond · The Australian Constitution
questions.questionText: What is the constitutional classification of New South Wales under the Australian Constitution?
questions.subtext: Distinguish between Australian States and Australian Territories.

options.text: It is a self-governing mainland Territory of the Commonwealth
It is one of the six original States of the Commonwealth of Australia
It is an independent sovereign monarchy
It is a foreign overseas protectorate administered under UN trust

statutoryGuidance.clue: New South Wales is classified as an Australian State.
statutoryGuidance.legalCitation: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, Section 6
statutoryGuidance.mnemonic: New South Wales = State.
statutoryGuidance.dossierNotes: The Australian federation consists of six original States and two major mainland Territories.
